deliverables.text: A ranking from Appendix B: top three centuries per reading with values; both readings' values for both winning centuries; the gap between the two winners on each reading as a percent of the larger value.
A box-and-whisker plot of dates per site from Appendix C with five-number summary, IQR, fences, outlier count and mean dates per site, plus a sentence on what outliers could do to the Dates reading.

A table of five cuts (centuries from 0, centuries shifted 50, median, mean and mode single-year shortcuts): winner on each reading, its lead over the runner-up as a percent of the winner, whether the readings agree, and which D1 findings survive every cut.

A weighted score (1 - s) x dates score + s x sites score for the two winning centuries, the scores at s = 0.5, the tie weight, the student's defended s, and a wall sentence of 20 words or fewer with two defending sentences.

balance.argument_a: The Dates reading is the field-standard summed probability and 700-799 leads it by 10.15% (272.0 vs 244.4; 18.2% over 1100-1199). The Sites reading counts a one-date site (358 of 863 sites) as much as a deeply studied one; among the 87 sites with 10 or more dates, 700-799 leads both readings (dates 154.6 vs 88.4, sites 38.4 vs 36.6). At weights s below 0.389 the blended score favours A.
balance.argument_b: The Sites reading leads by 15.93% (152.5 vs 128.2), more than A's 10.15% lead; 1200-1299 is second on Dates while 700-799 is fifth on Sites. The Dates lead is carried by a few heavily dated sites (the heaviest supplies 39.2 of 272.0 in 700-799), and a cluster bootstrap has it ahead in only about 71% of resamples against about 98% for the Sites lead. At weights s above 0.389 the blended score favours B (3.05% at s = 0.5).
balance.margin_basis: margin = (winner - loser)/winner on the blended score at s = 0.5: A = 0.5 x 1.0000 + 0.5 x 0.8407 = 0.9203; B = 0.5 x 0.8985 + 0.5 x 1.0000 = 0.9493; (0.9493 - 0.9203)/0.9493 = 3.05% (3.04% unrounded). Per-reading margins: Dates 10.15% for A's century, Sites 15.93% for B's century; both inside the 20% cap.
balance.winner: B (Sites Wall) at s = 0.5; A below s = 0.389
balance.twist_effect: Two withheld analyses of the same release. Part 1, set aside the single most heavily dated site (137 dates): with centuries from 0 the Dates winner becomes 1200-1299 (241.1 vs 232.8) and the readings agree; blended at s = 0.5 B wins by 9.73%; with centuries shifted 50 the Dates winner stays 650-749 (250.8 vs 228.7). Part 2, keep only the 87 sites with 10 or more dates: both readings name 700-799 (dates 154.6 vs 88.4, sites 38.4 vs 36.6); blended at s = 0.5 A wins by 23.76%, flipping the base winner. Each reading depends on which sites are in the sample.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: M5 is a value judgment about what 'busiest' should mean on a public wall; no amount of research gives its true value. The mechanical +/-50% sweep flips the verdict (s = 0.25 gives A by 3.79%; s = 0.75 gives B by 9.66%) with margins well inside the 20% cap. Disclosed in FACILITATOR.md as the case's central fragility: the case's real answer is the student's defended weight, with tie at s = 0.389.

facilitator.twist: Two withheld analyses (same release): (1) set aside the heaviest-dated site, Dates winner moves to 1200-1299 and the readings agree under centuries from 0, but not under centuries shifted 50; (2) keep only the 87 sites with 10+ dates, both readings name 700-799 and the base winner flips to A.

context_glossary.desc: A lab measurement of how much carbon-14 remains in a sample of once-living material, such as charcoal or seeds. It gives an age in radiocarbon years that must be calibrated to become calendar years.

A reference curve built from records of known age, such as tree rings, that converts radiocarbon years into calendar years. Because it wiggles, one radiocarbon age can map to a spread of calendar years.
Calendar years before 1950 CE. 700 cal BP is about 1250 CE.
A place where people left traces of past activity, studied by archaeologists. Many sites matter to Native communities today.
